input: Compare guardrails vs app logic: why separate, testable, pluggable wrappers instead of hardcoding?
actual_output:
- Guardrails are cross-cutting concerns (like logging or authorization). They apply across many parts of the app (input, retriever, generator, etc.), so hardcoding them everywhere causes duplication and risk of missing places.

- Putting guardrails in a separate layer (a guard object with plugable validators) makes them pluggable and composable: you can add, remove, reorder, or replace validators without rewriting the app logic.

- Separate guardrails act on a contract, not on implementation details. That keeps the app and guard logic decoupled (they are related but separate entities), reducing coupling and accidental breakage when you change one side.

- Independent testing: you can test guardrails by themselves to ensure rules work, instead of only testing within the full app. That prevents false confidence from app-level tests and makes validation repeatable.

- Practical workflow reason: you iterate and improve the app via evaluation and observability first. If you hardcode guardrails early, you’ll have to reapply or rework them across final iterations. Keeping them as a wrapper means you add them after stabilizing app behavior.

- Reusability: a rule like “no toxic output” can then be reused across different apps (RAG, agents, chatbots) without modifying each implementation.

Keeping them as a **wrapper/layer** instead of hardcoding them gives these benefits:
- **Avoids breaking app code** when guardrails change
- **Prevents missed enforcement** across input, retriever, generator, etc.
- **Makes guardrails independently testable**
- **Keeps them pluggable and composable** so you can add, remove, or reorder validators without rewriting the app
- **Lets you improve or evaluate guardrails separately** from the application

In short, app logic handles the core workflow, while guardrails validate it against rules/specs as a separate, reusable layer.

- Run 1–3 baseline runs with the same config to measure compute noise (std dev).
- Run several config variations (4–8, ideally more) to get historical std dev.
- Save the computed thresholds/scores in thresholds.json.
- Reuse those thresholds to detect regressions — if a previously passing test now fails beyond the thresholds, it’s a regression.

input: Compare MLOps and LLMOps: models, workflows, and operational differences.
actual_output:
Models
- ML/DL models: usually trained by you as part of the project. They are more deterministic — for a given input they tend to give the same output. ML Ops focuses on training, evaluation, versioning and managing those model and data artifacts.
- LLMs: probabilistic by nature and often already available as pre-trained models you use in your app. LLM Ops centers the LLM as the core component and treats the model as part of the runtime application rather than something you always train from scratch.

Workflows
- ML Ops workflows: mostly a model pipeline + data pipeline. You train, evaluate, version and deploy a model; prediction is typically a single-step operation (input → model → output).
- LLM Ops workflows: often multi-step and application-driven. You build workflows around the LLM (prompt chains, orchestration, preprocessing steps, adapters, etc.). Workflow length and step count can vary a lot, and the LLM Ops requirements change with that complexity.

Operational differences
- Determinism vs probabilism: ML systems are less dynamic at inference time; LLMs produce variable outputs, so operations must handle nondeterminism (monitoring, validation, guardrails).
- Role of the model: ML Ops manages model training/evaluation life cycle; LLM Ops wraps operational practices, tools and processes around an existing LLM so organizations can use it reliably.
- Practices and tooling: ML Ops emphasizes dataset/model versioning, training pipelines and artifact tracking. LLM Ops emphasizes orchestration around the LLM, prompt engineering, fine-tuning/adapter use, monitoring, deployment and end-to-end application operations.
- Dynamism: LLM Ops is more dynamic — the runtime behavior and workflow complexity drive different operational criteria. ML Ops is complex but generally less dynamic at prediction time.

Summary
- ML Ops = manage training/evaluation/versioning of (mostly deterministic) ML/DL models and their data pipelines.
- LLM Ops = operate, orchestrate and monitor probabilistic LLMs inside application workflows, adapting operations to varying workflow complexity and runtime variability.

- **MLOps** is centered around a **trained machine learning model**. You start with a dataset, use **input features** and a **target feature**, train the model, evaluate it, and manage versioning and deployment. The workflow is more fixed and less dynamic.
- **LLMOps** is centered around **LLM-based applications**. The model is usually already available, and the main task is to build a **workflow or application around it**. This workflow can vary in length and complexity, so the operational needs also change.
- In **MLOps**, the core focus is **model training, evaluation, and productionizing the model**.
- In **LLMOps**, the core focus is **orchestrating the application workflow around the model**, which is much more dynamic.

So, in short: **MLOps manages model-centric systems; LLMOps manages application/workflow-centric systems built on top of existing LLMs.**

input: How do NOOP, error logging, and auto-fix differ for PII-detected failures?
actual_output:
- NOOP (no operation): do nothing to the input/output — the detected PII remains unchanged. The validation failure is recorded in Guardrails’ history (so you keep an audit trail), but no remediation is applied.

- Error logging: explicitly record/store the validation failure (for auditing, monitoring, or later review). Like NOOP, logging does not itself fix the PII; it just saves the failure information.

- Auto-fix (redactic text / redact): the validator applies a fix to the content (for example redaction or removal of the PII). The output is modified to remove or mask the sensitive data so the failure is corrected.

- **NOOP**: takes no action on the failed input; the value passes through unchanged.
- **Error logging**: does not change the input, but records the failure, including the reason and details like the error span/character index.
- **Auto-fix**: tries to correct the failed input and returns a modified, fixed value.

input: How does the fact-extraction LLM differ from judge LLM, and when is each used?
actual_output:
Fact-extraction LLM
- Role: take an expected output (answer key) and decompose it into individual claims or facts.
- What it does: extracts units of information (facts) from the expected answer. It does not compare or score anything.
- When used: in the extraction step, before any verification. Example in the context: it extracted 5 facts from the expected output (or in another example, 20 units were extracted).

Judge LLM
- Role: act as a verification system that compares facts (or retrieved context) to the query and judges relevance and correctness.
- What it does: for each fact it gets (one fact + the query), it decides whether that fact is relevant / whether the answer is hidden in that fact. It then reports relevance, gives a score, and explains the reason for the score.
- When used: after fact extraction and/or after retrieval — during the comparison/verification phase when you want to evaluate another LLM’s response (for example a RAG application output).

Main difference (simple)
- Fact-extraction LLM = produce facts from the expected output (no comparison).
- Judge LLM = compare those facts (or retrieved items) to the question/response, decide relevance, and give scores and reasons.

The **judge LLM** is used later to **compare those extracted claims against the retrieved context** and decide whether each claim is **supported/attributable** by the retriever’s output.

So:
- **Fact-extraction LLM** = extracts claims from the expected output
- **Judge LLM** = checks whether those claims appear in the retrieved context and evaluates recall/coverage

  - Human: slow — creating and annotating datasets by humans is time consuming.
  - LLM: fast — LLMs can generate datasets quickly from your knowledge base via a pipeline.

- Scalability
  - Human: not scalable — human annotation does not scale for repeated or frequent evaluations.
  - LLM: scalable — LLM-generated datasets can be produced at scale across many iterations.

- Reproducibility
  - Human: hard/expensive to reproduce frequently because of time and cost constraints.
  - LLM: reproducible — you can rerun the generation workflow to get datasets across iterations.

Caveat (important): LLM outputs are probabilistic and non-deterministic, and generation should follow a proper workflow. You may still need human checks for correctness or edge cases.

input: How do generation, filtration, and evolution turn synthetic goldens into realistic QA pairs, and why style output?

This uses an LLM to make examples more interesting, realistic, and harder to distinguish from human-made goldens (targeting roughly 80–90% similarity).  
Styling formats the evolved inputs and outputs (the way questions and answers are presented) so the QA pairs match real‑world formats and application needs — making them more realistic and usable for testing.

input: What is faithfulness, and how is its score computed from grounded/total claims?
actual_output:
Faithfulness measures how much the model's output is grounded in the retrieved context (i.e., how many output claims come from the context rather than the model's internal knowledge).

How the score is computed:
- Extract all factual claims from the model's output (total claims = denominator).
- For each claim, check against the retrieved context: verdicts can be Yes (grounded), No (hallucinated), or I don't know (ambiguous / unverifiable).
- Faithfulness score = (number of grounded claims) / (total number of claims).

Example: if there are 10 claims and 8 are grounded, score = 8/10 = 0.8 (80% faithful, 20% hallucination).

Notes from the context:
- Ambiguous ("I don't know") claims can be included or excluded in the calculation; including them lowers the score.
- You can change the truth-extraction limit, which affects the total claims counted and thus the ratio.

input: What are retriever failures, plus metrics and tunable params for each?
actual_output:
Retriever failures (3), the metric for each, and tunable params:

1) Coverage / completeness
- What it is: how much of the total relevant context the retriever can fetch.
- Metric: contextual recall.
- Tunable params: chunking hyperparameters (chunk size, overlap), topk (how many candidates you retrieve), embedding model / embedding stage.
- Tuning direction (from context): if recall is low → increase chunk size (and/or increase topk).

2) Relevancy
- What it is: how relevant the retrieved results are to the query.
- Metric: contextual relevancy.
- Tunable params: chunking hyperparameters (chunk size, overlap), embedding model, topk.
- Tuning direction (from context): if relevancy is low → decrease chunk size.

3) Ranking / order
- What it is: how well the retriever orders results by relevance.
- Metric: precision (used to measure ranking/order).
- Tunable params: reranker (add or tune a cross-encoder reranker), embedding model, topk, chunking choices.
- Note from context: a reranker (cross-encoder) can recalculate similarities and improve ranking.

General notes from the context:
- Chunking and the embedding stage are the main places to tune because they affect the retriever.
- Metrics are applied together across the application but target different components, so you can tweak the specific component the metric points to.

input: Compare CodeDeploy agent duties on EC2 vs ASG after a new deployment.
actual_output:
They are basically doing the same job, but in different runtime contexts.

Common duties (EC2 or ASG):
- Continuously poll the CodeDeploy service and ask “is there a new deployment?”
- When a new deployment is detected, get triggered and run the scripts/instructions defined in the app spec (app spec.yml / apps.yaml).
- Execute the actual commands on the instance (install Docker/CLI, run validations, start the application, etc.).
- In short: CodeDeploy creates the deployment, but the agent on the instance runs the scripts and performs the deployment actions.

ASG-specific context:
- Instances are launched from a launch template (OS, pre-installed software, etc.) according to the Auto Scaling Group desired capacity.
- The CodeDeploy agent is installed on those instances (via the launch template or pre-baked AMI) and will start working as each new instance comes up.
- The agent performs the same polling and script-running duties on each auto-launched instance, so deployments apply automatically as ASG instances are created.

Summary: duty-wise there’s no difference — both agents poll CodeDeploy and run appspec scripts — the difference is that with an ASG the instances (and their agents) are created/terminated automatically from a launch template, so the agent’s work happens as part of instance lifecycle scaling.

- **On ASG:** the agent runs on each instance in the group, so CodeDeploy can deploy across multiple instances automatically.

input: Compare Prometheus static configs vs EC2 service discovery for ASG targets in YAML; explain why static fails.
actual_output:
Static configs
- You list full endpoint addresses (IP/host) in prometheus.yml.
- Works only when endpoints are fixed and known ahead of time.
- Fails for an Auto Scaling Group because instances and their IPs are dynamic: new instances are created, others terminate, IPs can change. A static list becomes stale and won’t contain the current targets.

EC2 service discovery (ec2_sd_configs)
- Prometheus queries EC2 to discover targets instead of relying on a hard-coded list.
- Discovery is done by instance metadata and tags (you typically tag ASG instances and use those tags to find targets).
- Prometheus uses EC2 DescribeInstances and reads fields like private IP (default), availability zone, tags, state, etc. You can change to public IP via relabeling.
- Requires an IAM policy (DescribeInstances) attached to the role of the EC2 where Prometheus runs so it can retrieve instance metadata.

Why static fails for ASG targets
- ASG instances are ephemeral and their addresses change; you can’t maintain an accurate static list.
- Traffic/load balancing and autoscaling actions mean targets appear/disappear automatically, so scraping must adapt automatically.
- Service discovery handles this by tracking instances dynamically (via tags and EC2 metadata), so Prometheus always scrapes the current set of targets.
